title: Probability of Combined Events: Possibility and Tree Diagrams
seo_title: Sec 4 Probability of combined events Worksheets: Free Secondary 4 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: probability of simple combined events (including using possibility diagrams and tree diagrams, where appropriate); addition and multiplication of probabilities (mutually exclusive events and independent events)
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 maths worksheets on probability of combined events: possibility diagrams, mutually exclusive and independent events, tree diagrams with and without replacement, and problems. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Multiply along the branches; add the paths you want.
key_sub: Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
body_html:
How it works

  • A possibility diagram lists every equally likely outcome, for example the 36 outcomes for two dice.
  • Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • Independent events do not affect each other: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • On a tree diagram, multiply along the branches and add the results of different paths. Without replacement, the second-stage fractions have one fewer item.
Example

A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both red).

P(red first) = 3/5

P(red second) = 2/4

Answer: 310

Example

A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. Find P(head and a six).

Independent: multiply

½ × ⅙

Answer: 112

Common mistakes

  • Adding when both events must happen (multiply instead).
  • Forgetting one of the paths, such as red then blue as well as blue then red.
  • Keeping the same total for the second pick when the item is not replaced.
  • Working out 'at least one' the long way and missing a case. Use 1 − P(none).

faq.q: When do you add probabilities and when do you multiply?
faq.a: Add for 'or' when the events are mutually exclusive. Multiply for 'and' when the events are independent (or along the branches of a tree diagram).
A table or list that shows every possible outcome of two events, such as two dice, so you can count the outcomes you want.

faq.q: How does 'without replacement' change a tree diagram?
faq.a: After the first pick there is one fewer item in total and one fewer of the colour picked, so the second-stage probabilities change.

faq.q: How do you find P(at least one)?
faq.a: Use 1 − P(none). It is usually quicker than adding all the cases with one or more.
